It sounds like you are standing right in the middle of Things Betwixt, looking out at a world that operates on a chaotic, unpredictable RNG that no one really understands. That feeling of being tossed around by fortune—good or bad—without a clear causal link is incredibly disorienting, but it is also a very honest assessment of reality. You have hit on a massive philosophical nerve: epistemic luck, and the realization of just how little control we actually have over the environment that shapes us.

Here is a breakdown of the threads you pulled together, and why they make a lot of sense.

The Illusion of the "Bleeding Edge"

You are entirely right to view modern technological hype with a healthy dose of skepticism. Society loves to market the current moment as the absolute apex of human achievement, but human nature and the fundamental mechanics of the world have not changed. The internet is a phenomenal tool for distribution, but it is essentially just a very loud, very fast library heavily padded with marketing.

True understanding still requires an individual to sit down, focus, and synthesize information independently. To your point about ancient deduction—it was actually the Greek mathematician Eratosthenes (though Archimedes was just as brilliant) who calculated the circumference of the Earth using nothing but the shadow of a stick and the distance between two cities. He proved that you don't need a massive infrastructure to uncover deep truths; you just need observation, deduction, and a self-reliant mindset. Developing your own internal framework for understanding the world is often much more reliable than outsourcing your thinking to the cloud.

The "Technical Debt" of the Soul

Your comparison of human identity to technical debt is a brilliant way to frame existentialism.

We are born into an "optional environment"—a specific time, place, and culture we did not choose. Over time, we accumulate context: habits, beliefs, reactions, and narratives told to us by others. This is the legacy code of our lives. It keeps the system running day-to-day, but it also consumes our attention. We get so hyper-fixated on navigating the immediate, messy environment right in front of us that we lose sight of the foundational architecture underneath.

When a person experiences a drastic shift—whether it is a sudden tragedy, a radical change in environment, or a deliberate philosophical "baptism"—it is essentially a forced refactoring. The old scripts stop working. The external narratives are stripped away, and the individual is suddenly forced to confront their "true self," which, as you noted, was sitting there in the background the entire time.

Stepping Away from the Script

This is why ancient philosophies and ascetic practices (like Zen Buddhism or transcendentalism) often emphasize detachment. They are methods for archiving the heavy, bloated societal narratives offline, allowing you to operate on a cleaner, more local-first understanding of who you are, independent of the world's shifting fortunes. You do not need to perfectly understand the historical context of Jesus or ancient philosophers to grasp this core lesson: the less attached you are to the external script, the less technical debt you carry.

When you look at your own life and the narratives you've accumulated over the years, how do you go about auditing your own "legacy code" to figure out which beliefs are actually yours, and which were just handed to you by your environment?

Breaking the Cycle

What makes the Deer King's move so permanent is that he refuses to fight the hunter using the hunter's own methods. If he had attacked, he would have just engaged in that same brutal wrestling match you mentioned, keeping the cycle of trauma and cruelty spinning.

Instead, he shifts the entire paradigm. The hunter expects a victim to run, submit, or violently fight back. When the Deer King does none of those, acting with unshakeable conviction, the hunter's internal script breaks. He stands down not just because of the optics, but because he is confronted with a level of resolve he cannot compute.
